reasoning: In the only state-specific general-election polling for Alabama’s 2026 U.S. Senate race within the last 45 days, Barry Moore (R) leads Everett Wess (D) by 15 points, 47%–32%, indicating a strongly Republican-leaning contest at this stage.[1][12][13] No recent state-specific general-election presidential polling for Alabama was found in that period, so the current measurable margin applies to the Senate race only, consistent with the state’s R+15 Cook Partisan Voting Index.[3]

sources.name: Montgomery Advertiser
sources.details: Montgomery Advertiser reports a statewide poll of 601 likely Alabama voters showing Republican Senate nominee Barry Moore at 47% and Democrat Everett Wess at 32%, a 15-point Republican lead, with about 20% undecided.

sources.name: Politically.com / yes. every kid.
sources.details: Politically.com reproduces the same "yes. every kid." statewide Alabama survey results for the 2026 U.S. Senate race, with Barry Moore at 47% and Everett Wess at 32%, confirming a 15-point Republican advantage.

sources.name: Pollsmax
sources.details: Pollsmax aggregates Alabama’s 2026 U.S. Senate polling and reports a current polling average of 47% R to 32% D, an R+15 margin between Barry Moore and Everett Wess, based on the July 11 "yes. every kid." poll.

sources.name: PredictionMarketsPicks
sources.details: PredictionMarketsPicks reports that Barry Moore is trading at 97¢ in Alabama’s 2026 Senate prediction market, implying roughly a 97% chance of a Republican win, but does not provide a specific vote-margin estimate.
sources.date_range: As of August 15, 2026 (market snapshot, no field dates)

sources.name: Montgomery Advertiser (Trump approval context)
sources.details: The same Montgomery Advertiser statewide survey also measures Trump’s job approval in Alabama (53% approve, 40% disapprove), a contextual indicator of the state’s Republican tilt but not a direct presidential ballot test.

sources.name: Cook Partisan Voting Index (state context)
sources.details: The Cook Partisan Voting Index lists Alabama as R+15 at the statewide level, meaning its two-party presidential vote has been 15 points more Republican than the national average.
sources.date_range: Structural index based on 2020 and 2024 presidential results (no specific field dates)
